newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Vereinsbank CEO sees Bonn-Buba reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Vereinsbank CEO sees Bonn-Buba reconciliation.

text.p: Bayerische Vereinsbank AG chief executive Albrecht Schmidt said on Tuesday he envisaged some reconciliation between Bonn and the Bundesbank in their row over revaluing gold reserves.

Schmidt told Reuters he regarded efforts to ensure countries hit Maastricht convergence criteria on the nail to be unnecessary, since proof of commitment to stability among euro zone countries was far more important than numbers.
"I am unhappy and angry about the (euro) discussions at present," Schmidt said.
"We are looking at the frame, not at the picture and the picture is one of a converging Europe."
He said, however: "I don't think this debate is damaging in the long term, but unnecessary. I am totally certain that they (the government) will reach an agreement with the Bundesbank."
Schmidt was speaking on the fringes of the International Monetary Conference in Switzerland, where German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday defended his plan to revalue German gold reserves.
Bonn wants to revalue gold and currency reserves held at the Bundesbank nearer to market values and take a transfer from the extraordinary profit generated this year and next.

Schmidt said the debate over revaluing reserves, in what some analysts considered a bid to help Germany qualify for monetary union, and which has prompted charges of creative accounting and calls for Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign, was regrettable.

The Bundesbank has rejected the revaluation plan as an infringement of its autonomy and has said the procedure should be delayed until 1998 at the earliest or until after the euro is launched in 1999.
Waigel said on Monday he wanted to reach an agreement with the Bundesbank on the issue.

Schmidt said he was confident that Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) would get off the ground as planned on January 1, 1999 and praised efforts by Italy and Spain to get their finances in order to make the grade.
However, he said he could imagine a two-tier EMU launch, with countries not ready to participate in the 1999 launch joining in 2001, when the euro coins and notes are circulated.
He said it was important that those not included in the launch be given a fixed timetable for entry to the euro zone, rather than being left uncertain.
